segments.text: Why does Greenland look enormous beside Africa on Mercator maps? The projection magnifies high latitudes, not actual land.
Greenland covers about two point one seven million square kilometers. Africa covers thirty point four million: roughly fourteen times as much area.
On a globe, meridians converge toward the poles. Distances between neighboring lines of longitude get smaller.
Mercator draws meridians as equally spaced parallel lines. This stretches east-west distances more at high latitudes.
To preserve local angles, north-south distances must stretch equally. That is why latitude lines spread apart.
Consider a tiny patch at sixty degrees latitude, in a spherical model with scale one at the equator.
Locally, width doubles and height doubles: four times the area. This is not one factor for all Greenland.
Watch Greenland move south. We rotate its boundary rigidly on a sphere, then redraw it on this fixed Mercator map.
Its spherical area stays unchanged. The outline looks smaller near the equator because the map magnifies it less.
Mercator is not simply wrong. It preserves local angles, useful for expressing compass headings.
A constant-heading route becomes a straight line on Mercator. It is usually not the shortest path across the globe.
For comparing areas, choose an equal-area projection such as Equal Earth. Greenland and Africa now have their correct relative areas.
Equal Earth changes shapes and angles. No flat map avoids every kind of distortion.
Need to compare land area, or follow a compass heading? Choose the projection for that purpose.
